title: Digital Ethics, the Law and the Planet

pages.c08-p01: Explain what ethics means in digital technology and weigh up the benefits and harms (trade-offs) of a technology
pages.c08-p02: Describe intellectual property and copyright: what is protected, for how long, and when fair dealing allows limited use
pages.c08-p03: Compare licences for digital content: all rights reserved, Creative Commons, public domain, proprietary and open-source software
pages.c08-p04: Credit sources correctly with citations and a reference list, and explain how to avoid plagiarism
pages.c08-p05: Discuss who owns content made by generative AI and whether training AI on artists' work is fair, considering different viewpoints
pages.c08-p06: Describe the principles of the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 and the rights people have over their personal data
pages.c08-p07: Explain in simple terms what the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes illegal, and identify which law applies in a given situation
pages.c08-p08: Describe the environmental costs of digital technology, including data centres, the energy and water used by cloud services and AI, e-waste and rare minerals
pages.c08-p09: Estimate the energy use of devices and suggest greener digital habits and sustainable design choices
pages.c08-p10: Use a structured ethical decision framework to debate a technology case study and justify a conclusion

q.q: What does ethics mean in digital technology?
o: Deciding what is right and wrong in how technology is made and used
The rules Parliament makes about how computers may be sold
The study of how computer hardware processes data
A set of company policies for using school computers
q.why: Ethics is about right and wrong; laws are the rules made by Parliament.

q.q: Which statement about the law and ethics is correct?
o: Anything that is legal must also be ethical
Anything that is unethical is also against the law
The law and ethics always change at the same speed
Something can be legal but still be unethical
q.why: For example, posting an unkind but legal photo of a friend without asking.

q.q: What is a trade-off?
o: Swapping one device for a newer model
A law that controls online trading
Gaining something but losing something else
A benefit that has no downside at all
q.why: New technology usually brings benefits and harms together.

q.q: A smart doorbell records people walking past on the footpath. What are those passers-by?
o: Customers of the doorbell company
Stakeholders affected by the technology
Programmers of the doorbell
Owners of the recorded footage
q.why: Anyone affected by a technology is a stakeholder, even if they never chose it.

q.q: A school moves all homework online. Which group is most likely to be left out?
o: Teachers who mark work on the school system
Pupils with no laptop or reliable broadband at home
Pupils who already use the school app daily
Parents who check homework on their phones
q.why: Asking who a design leaves out shows the harm side of the trade-off.

q.q: Which question best checks who a design works for?
o: Who benefits, and who might be harmed or left out?
How fast does the new system run on a laptop?
How much did the developers pay for hosting?
Which programming language was it written in?
q.why: TransformED asks pupils to consider who a design works for, not just whether it works.

q.q: Self-service checkouts shorten queues. Which is a possible harm?
o: Customers spend less time waiting to pay
Shops can open more tills in the same space
Card payments are processed more quickly
Fewer jobs and harder use for some customers
q.why: The other options are benefits, not harms.

q.q: A pupil writes: 'Social media is simply bad.' Why is this a weak answer?
o: It is too long for an exam answer
It uses the wrong technical vocabulary
It ignores the benefits, so it does not weigh up both sides
Social media is not a digital technology
q.why: Most technologies are both helpful and harmful; good answers weigh both.

q.q: Which of these is an ethical issue rather than mainly a legal one?
o: Selling copies of a film you do not own
Hacking into a teacher's email account
Posting a friend's embarrassing photo without asking
Sharing customers' bank details online
q.why: The photo may not break a law, but it is unkind; the others are clearly illegal.

q.q: What is intellectual property?
o: Any physical object that a person owns
Creations of the mind, such as writing, music, inventions and logos
Software that has been bought with a licence
Personal data stored about a pupil
q.why: Intellectual property covers creations of the mind.

q.q: How does a story you write get copyright protection in the UK?
o: Automatically, as soon as it is created and recorded
By registering it and paying a fee
Only when the copyright symbol is added
Only once it has been published online
q.why: UK copyright is automatic; no registration or symbol is needed.

q.q: Which type of intellectual property protects a brand's logo?
o: Patent
Fair dealing
Design licence
Trade mark
q.why: Trade marks protect names, logos and slogans that identify a brand.

q.q: Which type of intellectual property protects a new invention?
o: Copyright
Trade mark
Creative Commons
Patent
q.why: Patents protect inventions and must be applied for.

q.q: Which UK law covers copyright?
o: Computer Misuse Act 1990
Data Protection Act 2018
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
q.why: The CDPA 1988 is the main UK copyright law.

q.q: For most books, songs and photos, how long does UK copyright last?
o: 50 years from the date it was made
The creator's lifetime plus 70 years
The creator's lifetime plus 20 years
70 years from the date it was made
q.why: Most works are protected for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years.

q.q: Which of these is NOT protected by copyright?
o: The idea for a game about building with blocks
The code written for a block-building game
The soundtrack recorded for the game
The artwork drawn for the game's menu
q.why: Copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself.

q.q: Which use is most likely to be fair dealing?
o: A teacher showing a short film clip to teach a point
A pupil uploading a full film to a public channel
A shop printing a famous painting on mugs to sell
A club copying a whole textbook for every member
q.why: Illustration for instruction allows small, fair use in teaching.

q.q: A pupil copies one diagram into private revision notes and writes the source. Why is this acceptable?
o: Anything found on a search engine is free to use
Diagrams are never protected by copyright
Revision notes are owned by the school
It is a small, credited use for private study
q.why: Private study is a fair dealing purpose when the amount is small and credited.

q.q: Saoirse credits a photographer under a photo on her band's website. Which is true?
o: Crediting the photographer makes any use legal
Band websites are exempt from copyright law
She still needs permission, because credit alone is not enough
Photos on websites are always public domain
q.why: Credit is good practice, but permission or a suitable licence is still needed.

q.q: Which statement about copyright is a common mistake?
o: Copyright protects computer code
If it is on Google, it is free to use
Copyright is automatic in the UK
Copyright can be licensed to others
q.why: Easy to find online does not mean free to use.

q.q: What is a licence for digital content?
o: A certificate showing a work is in the public domain
Permission from the owner to use a work, with conditions
A fee paid to the government to publish work
A list of every source used in a project
q.why: A licence gives permission, usually with conditions.

q.q: A web image says nothing about its licence. What should you assume?
o: All rights are reserved, so you must ask permission
It is in the public domain and free to use
It is licensed under CC BY by default
You may use it if you add a credit
q.why: All rights reserved is the default.

q.q: In a Creative Commons licence, what does BY mean?
o: You must buy the work first
You must not change the work
You must not make money from it
You must credit the creator
q.why: BY means Attribution: give credit.

q.q: In a Creative Commons licence, what does ND mean?
o: You must not download the work
You must not credit the work
You must not change the work
You must not share the work
q.why: ND stands for NoDerivatives: share it only as it is.

q.q: In a Creative Commons licence, what does SA require?
o: The work may only be used in the same country
The work must be shared without any credit
New versions must be shared under the same licence
The work may only be shared by schools
q.why: SA stands for ShareAlike.

q.q: A club wants an image for a poster selling tickets. Which licence would NOT allow this?
o: CC BY
CC BY-NC
CC BY-SA
Public domain
q.why: NC means NonCommercial, and selling tickets is commercial.

q.q: Which licence lets you use an image unchanged on a paid poster if you credit the creator?
o: CC BY-ND
CC BY-NC
CC BY-NC-ND
CC BY-NC-SA
q.why: CC BY-ND allows commercial use with credit, as long as the work is not changed.

q.q: Why are Beethoven's compositions in the public domain?
o: Beethoven chose a Creative Commons licence
Music cannot be protected by copyright
Orchestras paid to release them
Their copyright ran out long ago
q.why: Copyright expires after the creator's lifetime plus 70 years.

q.q: An orchestra's 2024 recording of a Beethoven symphony is best described as:
o: Public domain, because Beethoven's music is
Unprotected, because it is classical music
CC0, because it is based on old music
Protected, because the recording has its own copyright
q.why: A new recording of public domain music has its own copyright.

q.q: Which is an example of open-source software?
o: Microsoft Office
Adobe Photoshop
Firefox
Most console games
q.why: Firefox's source code is publicly available.

q.q: Which statement describes proprietary software?
o: Its code is shared for anyone to change
Its code is secret and you buy the right to use it
It has no copyright and anyone can copy it
It must always be given away for free
q.why: Proprietary software keeps its source code secret.

q.q: What is plagiarism?
o: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own
Quoting a source and citing it correctly
Using a Creative Commons image with credit
Writing a reference list in Harvard style
q.why: Plagiarism means passing off others' work as yours.

q.q: What is a citation?
o: A short note in the text showing where an idea came from
The full list of sources at the end of the work
A licence that lets you reuse an image
A summary of a source in your own words
q.why: A citation sits in the text, e.g. (BBC, 2025).

q.q: Where should a reference list go?
o: At the start of the work
In the file name of the work
In a separate email to the teacher
At the end of the work
q.why: The reference list gives full details at the end.

q.q: Why does a website reference include an accessed date?
o: It proves the website is not a fake site
It shows when the page was first written
Pages change, so it shows which version you read
It is needed for the citation to count
q.why: Online content changes over time.

q.q: In the Harvard style, which comes first in a website reference?
o: The web address
The author or organisation
The date accessed
The title of the page
q.why: Author (Year) Title. Available at: URL (Accessed: date).

q.q: A Wikipedia page has no named author. What goes in the author position?
o: Anonymous
Wikipedia
Unknown author
The page title
q.why: Use the organisation or website name when no person is named.

q.q: Which version avoids plagiarism?
o: The idea in your own words with a citation
The original sentence copied without a citation
The original with a few words swapped, uncited
The original sentence with the source's logo added
q.why: Paraphrasing properly means your own words plus a citation.

q.q: What do the letters TASL stand for when crediting an image?
o: Title, Address, Size, Link
Type, Author, Site, Language
Title, Age, Source, Location
Title, Author, Source, Licence
q.why: TASL is the recommended Creative Commons attribution.

q.q: A pupil used an AI chatbot to plan an essay. What should they do?
o: Nothing, because AI output has no author
Remove any sentences that sound like AI
Say which tool they used, when, and for what
Credit the AI as the author of the essay
q.why: Exam boards require AI use to be acknowledged.

q.q: Which reference is correctly written in Harvard style?
o: What is copyright? BBC. https://www.bbc.co.uk/example 2025 (Accessed: 3 March 2026)
https://www.bbc.co.uk/example (2025) BBC What is copyright? (Accessed: 3 March 2026)
BBC (2025) What is copyright? Available at: https://www.bbc.co.uk/example (Accessed: 3 March 2026)
BBC What is copyright? (Accessed: 2025) Available at: https://www.bbc.co.uk/example (3 March 2026)
q.why: Order: Author (Year) Title. Available at: URL (Accessed: date).

q.q: What is generative AI?
o: AI that only sorts data into categories
AI that creates new text, images, audio or video from a prompt
Software that generates electricity for servers
A program that copies files between devices
q.why: Generative AI makes new content.

q.q: What is training data?
o: The large set of examples an AI model learns patterns from
The answer an AI gives to a prompt
The licence that controls AI outputs
The electricity used to run an AI model
q.why: AI learns patterns from its training data.

q.q: What is a deepfake?
o: A very large hidden data centre
An AI model trained on deep-sea data
A virus that changes photo files
A realistic fake video, image or audio made with AI
q.why: Deepfakes can show real people saying or doing things they never did.

q.q: What is the main complaint many artists make about generative AI?
o: AI tools are too expensive for artists to buy
AI cannot produce images in colour
Artists are banned from using AI tools
Their work was used for training without permission or payment
q.why: Permission and payment are the main concerns.

q.q: In the USA, can an image made entirely by AI with no human author be copyrighted?
o: Yes, the AI company always owns it
Yes, if the prompt is long enough
No, because copyright needs a human author
Only if the image is printed on paper
q.why: US authorities have said purely AI-made work is not protected.

q.q: Which argument is often made by AI developers?
o: Creators should be paid for every training image
The AI learns patterns rather than storing copies of works
Companies should ask before using any work
AI should only be trained on public domain work
q.why: The others are arguments made by many creators.

q.q: What did the UK government's March 2026 report on AI and copyright do?
o: Dropped its preferred opt-out plan and asked for more evidence
Banned all AI training on copyright works
Made all AI output public domain
Required artists to register their styles
q.why: The report dropped the opt-out as its preferred option and called for more evidence.

q.q: Which is a possible compromise in the AI training debate?
o: Licensing deals where AI companies pay to use creators' work
Allowing AI firms to use any work with no conditions
Banning all generative AI everywhere
Letting AI companies decide all the rules
q.why: Licensing gives creators payment while allowing training.

q.q: Ella uses AI to create a mascot, then redraws it by hand for two hours. Which is most accurate?
o: The AI company automatically owns the whole design
Nobody can ever own anything that started with AI
The artists in the training data own her mascot
Her own hand-drawn changes strengthen her claim to own it
q.why: The more human creativity added, the stronger the claim.

q.q: Which is the best way to write about the AI ownership debate?
o: State your opinion as if it were a fact
Only describe the side you agree with
Give reasons for each side, then reach a justified view
Say there is no point discussing it
q.why: Debated issues need both sides with reasons.

q.q: Which of these is personal data?
o: The rules of Gaelic football
A pupil's name and home address
Average monthly rainfall in Belfast
The price of a games console
q.why: It can identify a living person.

q.q: Which laws protect personal data in Northern Ireland?
o: Computer Misuse Act 1990 only
UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
The WEEE Regulations
q.why: These apply across the whole UK.

q.q: A quiz app asks for your home address but does not need it. Which principle is broken?
o: Data minimisation
Accuracy
Accountability
Data portability
q.why: Only collect what you really need.

q.q: A club uses members' emails to sell holidays for another company. Which principle is broken?
o: Data minimisation
Storage limitation
Accuracy
Purpose limitation
q.why: Data must only be used for the reason it was collected.

q.q: A school keeps the wrong emergency phone number for a pupil. Which principle is broken?
o: Purpose limitation
Storage limitation
Accuracy
Transparency
q.why: Personal data must be correct and up to date.

q.q: What is a subject access request?
o: Asking a website to remove an advert
Asking a teacher for extra homework
Asking an organisation for a copy of your personal data
Asking the police to investigate hacking
q.why: It uses your right of access.

q.q: How long does an organisation normally have to reply to a subject access request?
o: One week
One month
Six months
One year
q.why: Normally one month, longer for very complicated requests.

q.q: Which statement about the right to erasure is correct?
o: You can ask for deletion, but it is not automatic
Organisations must always delete data when asked
It only applies to adults over 18
It means data must be deleted after one year
q.why: A school, for example, must keep some records by law.

q.q: Which body enforces data protection law in the UK from 30 September 2026?
o: The Information Commissioner's Office
The National Crime Agency
The Intellectual Property Office
The Information Commission
q.why: The Information Commission replaced the ICO on that date.

q.q: Which of these is extra-sensitive personal data?
o: A pupil's favourite school subject
The name of a pupil's form class
A pupil's lunch menu choice
A fingerprint scan used to unlock a door
q.why: Biometric data such as fingerprints has stronger protection.

q.q: Medical notes are left on a corridor printer. Which principle is broken?
o: Purpose limitation
Data portability
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
Accuracy
q.why: Personal data must be kept safe from being seen by the wrong people.

q.q: Which law makes hacking into an account illegal?
o: Data Protection Act 2018
Computer Misuse Act 1990
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
UK GDPR
q.why: Unauthorised access is a Computer Misuse Act offence.

q.q: Why was the Computer Misuse Act passed?
o: No law clearly covered hacking when two men hacked a BT system
Schools asked for rules on using computers in class
Too much personal data was being collected
Music was being copied onto computers
q.why: The 1980s BT hacking case showed a gap in the law.

q.q: Cian posts a joke from a friend's laptop that was left logged in. What is this?
o: Unauthorised access to computer material
Legal, because the account was already open
Fair dealing, because it was only a joke
A data protection breach by the friend
q.why: He used the account without permission.

q.q: Which is the key difference between ethical hacking and a crime?
o: Whether anything is damaged
The age of the person hacking
Whether the hacking was difficult
Permission from the system's owner
q.why: Authorised testing is legal; unauthorised access is a crime.

q.q: Paying a booter service to crash a rival's game server is which offence?
o: Unauthorised access only, with no damage
A breach of the data minimisation principle
An unauthorised act that impairs a computer
Copyright infringement of the game
q.why: Deliberately stopping a computer working impairs it.

q.q: Selling a keylogger designed to steal passwords is which offence?
o: Unauthorised access to computer material
Making or supplying tools for computer misuse
Breaking the storage limitation principle
Breaking a Creative Commons licence
q.why: Supplying tools for misuse is an offence under the Act.

q.q: Getting into someone's online banking in order to steal money is:
o: Only a breach of data protection law
Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences
Legal if the password was easy to guess
An unauthorised act that impairs a computer
q.why: Access in order to commit another crime is the more serious access offence.

q.q: What is the National Crime Agency's Cyber Choices scheme for?
o: Steering young people with cyber skills towards legal careers
Fining companies that lose personal data
Teaching pupils how to reference websites
Recycling old school computers safely
q.why: It aims to stop young people drifting into cyber crime.

q.q: A pupil shares a pirated copy of a new game online. Which law is mainly broken?
o: Computer Misuse Act 1990
Data Protection Act 2018
WEEE Regulations
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
q.why: Copying and sharing without permission is copyright infringement.

q.q: A hacker steals a shop's customer list. Why might the shop also be in trouble?
o: It owns the copyright in the customer list
It is responsible for the hacker's actions
It may not have kept the personal data secure
Shops cannot store any personal data
q.why: Keeping personal data secure is a data protection principle.

q.q: What is a data centre?
o: A shop that repairs broken laptops and phones
A school room with networked computers
A building full of servers that run online services
A cloud-based app for storing photos
q.why: The cloud runs on real data centres.

q.q: Why do many data centres use a lot of water?
o: To clean dust from the servers
To cool the hot servers
To generate their own electricity
To store data in water tanks
q.why: Water-based cooling is common.

q.q: According to the IEA, roughly what share of the world's electricity did data centres use in 2024?
o: About 1.5%
About 15%
About 0.01%
About 50%
q.why: The IEA estimated about 415 TWh, around 1.5% of global electricity.

q.q: What did the IEA project for data centre electricity use by 2030?
o: It will fall by half as chips improve
It will stay exactly the same as 2024
It will be replaced entirely by solar panels
It could roughly double, mostly because of AI
q.why: The IEA projected roughly double by 2030, driven largely by AI.

q.q: For many phones and laptops, which stage causes most of their carbon footprint?
o: Charging
Transport
Recycling
Manufacturing
q.why: Making the device is usually the biggest part.

q.q: What is a carbon footprint?
o: The amount of carbon used to build a circuit
The physical size of a data centre
The total greenhouse gases released because of something
The number of devices a person owns
q.why: It measures greenhouse gas emissions.

q.q: What does the crossed-out wheelie bin symbol on a device mean?
o: It is made from recycled plastic
Do not throw it in your normal bin
It is safe to burn the device
It uses no electricity at all
q.why: It is the WEEE symbol: recycle separately.

q.q: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reported roughly how much e-waste was produced in 2022?
o: About 62 million tonnes
About 62 thousand tonnes
About 6 million tonnes
About 620 million tonnes
q.why: About 62 million tonnes, with only about 22% properly recycled.

q.q: Why is dumping e-waste harmful?
o: Harmful substances like lead and mercury can leak out
E-waste quickly rots into plant food
E-waste uses electricity in landfill
E-waste creates new rare earth elements
q.why: Harmful substances pollute soil and water.

q.q: Using the rough example, a phone costs 60 kg of carbon to make and 2 kg a year to charge. What is the yearly footprint if kept for 4 years?
o: 32 kg a year
62 kg a year
15 kg a year
17 kg a year
q.why: 60 / 4 = 15, plus 2 for charging = 17 kg a year.

q.q: What is the formula for energy in kilowatt-hours?
o: Power in watts divided by hours, times 1000
Hours divided by power in watts
Power in watts times hours, divided by 1000
Power in watts times hours, times 1000
q.why: Watt-hours divided by 1000 gives kWh.

q.q: A 50 W laptop is used for 4 hours. How much energy does it use?
o: 200 kWh
0.2 kWh
2 kWh
0.02 kWh

q.q: A 150 W console is used for 3 hours a day. How much energy is that per day?
o: 450 kWh
0.45 kWh
4.5 kWh

q.q: A 120 W console is used for 2 hours a day for 30 days. How much energy is used?
o: 7.2 kWh
72 kWh
0.24 kWh
7200 kWh
q.why: 120 x 2 = 240 Wh = 0.24 kWh per day; x 30 = 7.2 kWh.

q.q: A pupil calculates 150 W x 3 hours = 450 kWh. What mistake have they made?
o: They should have divided by 3
They should have added, not multiplied
They forgot to multiply by 365
They forgot to divide by 1000
q.why: 450 is watt-hours; divide by 1000 for 0.45 kWh.

q.q: If electricity is assumed to cost 25p per kWh, what does 164.25 kWh cost?
o: About £4
About £410
About £41
About £16

q.q: Which habit usually saves the most carbon over time?
o: Deleting a single old email
Turning the phone's volume down
Keeping a phone for four years instead of two
Changing to a darker wallpaper once
q.why: Making a device causes most of its footprint.

q.q: Which is an example of sustainable design?
o: Gluing the battery in so it cannot be removed
Using screws so the battery can be replaced
Stopping security updates after one year
Adding large uncompressed images to a website
q.why: Design for repair makes devices last longer.

q.q: Why can efficient code help the environment?
o: It does the job with less processing, so uses less energy
It makes the program file look more colourful
It means the program never needs any updates
It lets the program run without electricity
q.why: Less processing across millions of devices saves energy.

q.q: Why use a decision framework for an ethical question?
o: To guarantee everyone agrees with the answer
To avoid thinking about other people's views
To replace the need to check the law
To think it through step by step so nothing is missed
q.why: A framework structures careful thinking.

q.q: What is usually the first step in the ethical decision framework?
o: Decide and justify
Vote on the answer
Check the environment
Establish the facts
q.why: Start with what is actually being proposed.

q.q: Which is the best compromise option for canteen facial recognition?
o: Make it compulsory for every pupil in the school
Let the technology company decide the rules
Make it optional with consent and keep cards available
Ban all payment technology from the canteen
q.why: A compromise keeps benefits while reducing harms.

q.q: Why is a leaked face scan more serious than a leaked PIN?
o: Face scans are easier to guess than PINs
You cannot change your face like a PIN
PINs are a type of biometric data
Face scans are not personal data
q.why: Biometric data is permanent.

q.q: What happened when some Scottish schools used facial recognition for lunch payments in 2021?
o: They paused it after privacy concerns
It became compulsory in every UK school
It was found to be fully lawful and expanded
It was replaced by fingerprint scanners everywhere
q.why: The schools paused it, and the regulator later said it likely broke data protection law.

q.q: In a debate, what is a rebuttal?
o: Answering the other side's arguments
The opening speech for the motion
The vote at the end of the debate
The statement being debated
q.why: Rebuttal responds to the other side's points.

q.q: What is the motion in a debate?
o: The final decision made by the teacher
The team that speaks against the idea
The evidence given by each speaker
The statement that the two sides argue for and against
q.why: e.g. This house believes schools should use facial recognition.

q.q: Which conclusion is best justified?
o: No, because I just do not like cameras
Yes, because technology is always progress
On balance no, because the privacy risk outweighs saving a few minutes
Yes, because the company said it was safe
q.why: It weighs the trade-off and gives a reason.

q.q: Which step checks whether an option respects privacy and consent?
o: Stakeholders
Law and rights
Facts
Options
q.why: The law and rights step checks legality, privacy and consent.
